title: A Giant Computer Model Lights Up the Universe's Dark Age
summary:
Imagine the early universe as a dark room with no lights on. Scientists call this time the cosmic dark age, and a powerful new computer simulation called Lumina is helping them explore it.

Scientists at MIT, Harvard, and other schools built Lumina. It recreates about 2 billion years of cosmic history across a region about 1.6 billion light-years wide and shows how the first galaxies formed.

The story starts with the Big Bang. As the universe cooled, electrons joined atomic nuclei to form hydrogen. About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the dark age began, with no stars yet to light it.

Then the first stars and galaxies appeared. Their ultraviolet light knocked electrons off hydrogen atoms, a change called re-ionization, and the universe grew clearer.

Lumina also follows helium re-ionization, a harder change that needs much stronger light. The results suggest feeding supermassive black holes supplied it, while stars and galaxies handled the hydrogen.

MIT physics professor Mark Vogelsberger says Lumina covers star and galaxy formation and the re-ionization of hydrogen and helium, in a space 100 times bigger than earlier simulations.

Lumina builds on an earlier simulation called IllustrisTNG, and the team is sharing it so other scientists can check its ideas against telescope observations.
why_it_matters: Just like turning on a light helps you find your way in a dark room, Lumina helps curious kids understand how the first stars lit up the universe we live in today.

background_read: The cosmic dark age was a time in the early universe when there were no stars yet, so space was dark.
A computer simulation is a model built by scientists to copy how something works, so they can study it even when they cannot see it directly.
Lumina is a powerful computer model that recreates how the first stars and galaxies formed and how their light changed the gas around them.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists at MIT, Harvard, and other schools, including MIT physics professor Mark Vogelsberger.
WHAT: They built Lumina, a powerful computer simulation that recreates about 2 billion years of cosmic history and shows how the first galaxies formed and how hydrogen and helium were re-ionized.
WHERE: In a simulated region about 1.6 billion light-years wide, a space 100 times bigger than earlier simulations covered.
WHY: To explore the cosmic dark age and let other scientists check its ideas about the early universe against telescope observations.
